14242-the-touchstone-of-fortune-being-th:
Charles Major's 1912 memoir novel follows Baron Clyde through the doleful reign of Charles II, the so-called Merry Monarch. Fortune, the narrator argues, smiles on a man who risks all on a desperate chance: losers look foolish, winners look lucky, but courage mints the coin. George Hamilton, penniless second son of a great house, supplies the proof.

Court scandal drives the plot. Frances and Nelly visit the Old Swan, where grilled lobster draws the narrator for lunch, and a maid's innocent tale to the king brings trouble to Frances and George. Secrecy becomes the only shield: Sarah suggests testifying that her sister stayed home since yesterday noon, with father and John Churchill to swear it. Charles Major writes Restoration intrigue with relish, and fortune's touchstone tests every character it meets.

the-touchstone-of-fortune-being-the-memo:
Charles Major's Touchstone of Fortune, dated 1912, purports to be the memoir of Baron Clyde, who lived and fell in the reign of Charles II. The narrator opens with Goddess Fortune, who smiles on men risking everything on a desperate chance; winners, he says, have simply minted their courage. His great example is George Hamilton, penniless younger son of the House of Hamilton, whose elder brother Count Anthony kept an eye on the crumbs from his table.

When Charles II was restored in 1660, Hamilton, who had shared the exile, became Second Gentleman of the Bedchamber at Whitehall. There he lived on pension, card winnings, and disreputable revenues in a court where debts went unpaid and vice was daily jest and pride. Major, author of When Knighthood Was in Flower, writes Restoration intrigue from inside a courtier's cynical memory.
